people.name: Fábio Schvartsman
people.summary: Vale chief executive from May 2017 until he took leave in March 2019. Charged with qualified homicide and environmental crimes over the 25 January 2019 Córrego do Feijão dam collapse, reported as killing 270 people (272 in one report). A regional court halted the case; Brazil's Superior Court of Justice put him back as a defendant in April 2026 and refused his appeal in June 2026. He has not been tried.

posts.years: May 2017-March 2019

records.what: Took leave from Vale in March 2019 after federal prosecutors recommended he leave the company immediately.
His defence filed a habeas corpus petition asking for the criminal case to be dismissed.

The Superior Court of Justice's Sixth Panel accepted the federal prosecutors' appeal on 7 April 2026, reversing the TRF6 regional court, which had suspended the case. Mining Reporters says the case is at a preliminary stage.
On 7 May 2026 the 2nd Federal Criminal Court of Belo Horizonte put him back in the criminal cases.

On 2 June 2026 the Sixth Panel unanimously rejected his defence's appeal and refused to suspend the cases. He faces two cases, one for environmental crimes and one for qualified homicide, the second under jury-trial rules. The defence had 100 days to answer the charges.

people.summary: Diamond and mining investor behind Beny Steinmetz Group Resources (BSGR), the group that Koidu Holdings belonged to when police shot two people dead at a 2007 protest at the Koidu mine in Sierra Leone. OCCRP reports he flew to Freetown in May 2008 and met the president, after which the government let the halted mine restart. He is not accused over the shootings. Separate matter, not part of this map case: Swiss courts convicted him of bribing foreign officials over iron ore rights in Guinea.

In May 2008, after police shot two people dead at a demonstration and the government halted Koidu, he flew to Freetown and met President Koroma. What was said was not disclosed. The government then dropped its demands and let Koidu restart.

Separate matter: the Swiss Federal Court upheld his conviction for bribing foreign officials in rulings dated 24 March 2025, finding he paid $8.5 million to Mamadie Touré, wife of Guinea's President Conté, between 2006 and 2012. people.name: Iskandar Safa
people.summary: Owner and chief executive of Privinvest, the shipbuilder paid under Mozambique's hidden loans. He died in January 2024. London's High Court found in July 2024 that he was "the individual ultimately behind each promise and payment" to finance minister Manuel Chang. This is a civil finding. The Court of Appeal struck out the Privinvest companies' appeal in May 2026 for failing to meet its terms.

posts.years: during the 2013-2014 loans

records.what: Former Credit Suisse bankers told US prosecutors they received kickbacks from him, among others.

The High Court ruled on 29 July 2024 that Mozambique was entitled to just over $825 million from Privinvest and Safa, plus cover for an estimated $1.5 billion still owed to lenders, and found bribes of at least $7 million were paid to Chang.

The Court of Appeal struck out Privinvest's appeal by an order dated 6 May 2026, because the group did not meet security terms, according to Mozambique's lawyers. The judgment is final against the Privinvest companies.
An appeal by his widow against being pursued for the claim was dismissed, reported 26 October 2026; the sum she may owe is not set. The report says he died in January 2024, aged 68.
